title: Muslims as minorities
hook: Muslims living as minorities, balancing faith and society

segments.voice: Yesterday, young Muslims, and your line: the young carry it. Did you say your sentence of encouragement out loud? Today closes this stretch of the path, a diverse ummah, with Muslims who live among neighbors of other faiths. Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

Umm Salamah remembers it in her own words, kept in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad. A small group of Muslims, pressed hard in Mecca, crossed the sea to Abyssinia, a Christian kingdom ruled by a king known by his title, the Negus. In paraphrase, she says: we came to the land of Abyssinia, and found there the best of neighbors, and we could practice our religion in safety. Then envoys arrived from Mecca to have them sent back. The king called the Muslims in and asked them to speak for themselves. A minority, in a strange land, standing before a king of another faith. Some of the Prophet's own companions were exactly that.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA TO ABYSSINIA.` → `THE BEST OF NEIGHBORS.` → `SPEAK FOR YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: First, how the story turns. Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, speaks for the group, and the king asks to hear something of their scripture. Ja'far recites from the opening of surah Maryam, about Mary and the birth of Jesus. Umm Salamah says the king wept until his beard was wet, and refused to hand them over. The minority was protected, and the scene is one of mutual respect. Second, the principle Muslims draw from texts like this. A verse of the Qur'an, in paraphrase, says Allah does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who have not fought you over religion or driven you from your homes, and that Allah loves those who deal justly. Third, the questions of daily life today. Muslims live as minorities in Europe and the Americas, in India and China, in Australia and across Africa. The questions are practical: where to pray at work, how to keep Friday prayer with a school schedule, finding halal food, Eid on a working day, a Muslim burial plot, and being misunderstood in the news. Some scholars have built a whole field around these questions, called the fiqh of minorities. Others hold that the classical schools already have what is needed. Both are trying to answer the same family's questions. Fourth, the balance itself. A Muslim nurse prays in a supply room on her break. A family explains Ramadan at a school meeting. A mosque opens its doors to the neighbors on Eid. Day to day, faith as a minority can look less like grand debates and more like these small, steady negotiations, made with a neighbor who may become, as Umm Salamah put it, the best of neighbors.
screen: `JA'FAR RECITES MARYAM; THE KING WEEPS.` · `KINDNESS AND JUSTICE TO NEIGHBORS.` · `PRAYER AT WORK, EID ON A WORKDAY.` · `SMALL, STEADY NEGOTIATIONS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one minority's story. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the small group arriving by sea in Abyssinia, carrying very little, not knowing who will welcome them. Hold that picture for a few breaths. Then let it move to today: a Muslim family in a town where theirs is the only hijab at the grocery store, or the only family skipping lunch through Ramadan. If you pray, you can ask for good for them, and for their neighbors, in your own words. Later today, read one account, in a Muslim's own words, of life as a minority somewhere. The bell holds the time.
Muslims as minorities. From companions sheltered in Abyssinia to families today in Europe, the Americas, India, China and beyond, keeping faith among neighbors of other faiths. Today's word.

Your line: faith as a minority. This stretch, a diverse ummah, gave us many ways of being Muslim: mosque, imam, Deobandi and Barelvi, Tablighi, Salafi, Sufi, Shia, Isma'ili, converts, women, hijab, the young, and minorities. Today, be someone's best of neighbors. Tomorrow, a new stretch: science and faith. Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims living as minorities pray at work or school where space allows, look for halal food and Muslim burial, arrange leave for Friday prayer and Eid, and often open their mosques to neighbors; some follow scholars of the 'fiqh of minorities', others the classical schools directly.
